utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I'd like to put on the record that we received an e-mail today at 1.25 p.m. We received it from Mr. Scott Martin, who adds to the information about the outstanding translations. There seems to be a disagreement between CLSS and the Stanisic Defence. And even if we take into account a few additional matters such as rejected documents, that still there is no full agreement on how many pages are outstanding or not. Also, the Chamber is, of course, not aware of the reasons for the rejection of certain documents. We were informed that they'll be -- that the Defence anticipates that they'll resubmit these documents. The e-mail also informs the Chamber that the Defence is currently investigating why there exists such a difference. The Chamber will ask, anyhow, for further submissions on the matter, on short notice. You will most likely receive an e-mail indicating that very soon. And we'll also ask for CLSS registry submissions under Rule 33(B) but also on very short notice in order not to lose any further time. Now, of course it would be helpful and the Chamber would encourage the Stanisic Defence to communicate with CLSS in such a way that it's clear where the disagreement lies, so that we don't have to spend too much time on that. And it's -- in general terms, if there is a disagreement between one of the teams, whether Prosecution or Defence, and one of the services of the registry, it's always preferred to first see whether -- to find out together what the basis of the disagreement is and to see how to resolve that. I put this already on the record, and the Chamber will, from -- I think that we'll request for further information still to be delivered this week, to be submitted this week, so that we can consider that further information. That might also include why the documents that were rejected, why they were rejected, because that is not explained in the -- in the e-mail. Then we move on. Is the Stanisic Defence ready to call its next witness? Yes. Now, we'll move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the first thing the Chamber intends to do if the closed session is effective, and we'll hear from Madam Registrar whether it is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. -- is to ask the witness whether he has any personal reasons for the protective measures which were requested by Serbia. I don't know whether you have any information about that. If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's why I was on my feet, Your Honour. The witness isn't asking for protective measures for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The witness isn't asking for protective measures for personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll tell him that he testifies with the protective measures exclusively because they were asked for by the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DST-074. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DST-074. Please be seated. Witness DST-074, we are in closed session, which means that no one sees or hears out -- outside this courtroom what we are saying. The protective measures in place also include face distortion and voice distortion, which means that the recording doesn't show your face. It's scrambled. And on the recording, at this moment at least, no one can hear your own voice. This is all done at the request of the Republic of Serbia. I was informed by Mr. Jordash, Defence counsel, that you had no personal reasons for asking for protective measures. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is accurate. I don't have any personal reasons to ask for protective measures. I'm not ashamed of what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then just for your information, the Chamber is seeking additional information from the Republic of Serbia. So the final decision on whether the content of your testimony will be public or not depends on the decision still to be taken by this Chamber on the basis of additional information we've asked for. So for you, don't be surprised if at any later stage your testimony will become public. That's also the reason why I asked you whether you had any personal reasons, but apparently you have not. Then, Mr. Jordash, are you ready to start your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps also for your information: Because of these protective measures, we do not call you by your own name. We call you Witness DST-074. But, again, it is possible that at a later stage your own name will become public. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic, and he'll start his examination. Now, Mr. Jordash, initially the witness was scheduled for two and a half hours viva voce, and now he's still on two and a half hours under 92 ter, which comes a bit as a surprise, but also looking at the rather extensive 92 ter statement. But I -- as always, I encourage you to be as efficient as possible, not to waste any time, and to be as focussed as possible as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will certainly do my best. Unfortunately, the pseudonym sheet isn't uploaded, but if I may hand out copies. And one copy for the witness, and for the Trial Chamber and the parties, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take care that it will be uploaded as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the document in front of you, which contains personal details, name, and date of birth, and confirm whether they are accurate?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The information on this sheet is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the pseudonym sheet would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be exhibit D333 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D333 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could document 1D5000 please be brought to the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, there's going to be a document on the screen - it's there now - purporting to be a statement given by you on the 25th of May, 2011, and the 5th of August, 2011. Do you recall giving a statement to members of the Stanisic Defence on those dates?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I gave the statement, I read it, and I signed it with my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I've just told you that I signed it with my own hand. This is, indeed, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you sign every page?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Each and every page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you've just said you have read it. Did you have a good opportunity to carefully review it before coming to court today, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: This is my statement. I dictated it, I read it, and if there was need to make any changes, I made them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen 1D4976.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall reviewing the statement we've just had on the screen and making amendments which were recorded in the document which you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. I signed that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apart from those changes, is there anything else that you wish to change in the first statement we saw on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the statement and the corrections which we have in front of us, are they in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I swore that I would be telling the truth. I did it before, and I can -- I intend to do so in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if asked the same questions in substance, would you give the same answers as you did within your statement and the corrections in the proofing note?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I told the truth. There's no reason why I shouldn't repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender the witnesses statement and the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to put on the record that this statement was disclosed on the 10th of August, which is approximately two months after the disclosure deadline provided for in Rule 67(A)(ii) and in the Chamber's order. The late disclosure of 92 ter statements in this case is an ongoing problem that the Chamber is well aware of and that the Defence acknowledges. It's a problem not just with respect to this statement but also with respect to witness statements from other witnesses who will testify about the same matters as this witness, since we don't yet know the entirety of the Defence case. It was our understanding based on counsel's representations prior to the recess that all 92 ter statements would be completed and disclosed before the end of the recess, but that doesn't appear to have happened. In this particular instance, and in the interest of efficiency, we don't object to the admission of this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter, but we reserve the right to ask for other relief if it later becomes apparent that other relief is required as a result of a late disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, your observations are on the record. Since the Defence does -- the Prosecution does not object to the admission of the statement and the proofing note, Madam Registrar, the number of the statement would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the number to be assigned to the proofing note would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D334 and D335 are admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we have, please, on the screen 1D4929.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before you, Mr. Witness, is a chart, as you can see. Do you recall being given in the last two days a number of documents to review with this chart, with a space for comments on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I got a file containing some documents. There was a chart in front of those documents. It contained the number of those documents. And whatever I knew with regard to each particular document, I noted in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to review the chart and make any clarifications or corrections that you wished to make?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I've just told it, that I provided all the information that I had with regard to each and every document. I recorded that information in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what you recorded was in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: This is what I know. This is the truth, and I adhere by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And these are the comments you'd make in relation to these documents, and these are the answers you'll give in relation to any questions on the documents?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I could tell you differently only if I wanted to lie. But I'm not here to lie. This is the truth. This is what I have noted. And this is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, could we have -- oh, could I tendered this chart. There is a number of objections or issues which need to be resolved before all the exhibits -- until the Prosecution withdraw any objections to a number of exhibits, but may I tender the chart and MFI it at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would just give me one moment to look at a few ... One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry, but I have to verify one thing. You called -- Mr. Jordash, you asked to have on the screen 1D4929, and that is a chart. At the same time, Madam Registrar informs me that 1D4929 was MFI'd as D327. I'm unable to verify that because what we see on our screen is a chart, so I'm slightly confused about the situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this isn't the right chart. This is for DST-043. This witness is DST-074, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so perhaps you need to invent another number to get the right chart on your -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar informs me that what was uploaded as a chart of exhibits for DST-074 as it is stated in the 12.15 p.m. e-mail on the 16th of August is that the chart is 1D04977. So if that's the chart you'd like to be shown on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we lost two minutes, but at least we avoided further confusion. Madam Registrar, could we have 1D04977 on the screen. Is this the right chart, Mr. Jordash? It looks as if it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise the comments against the description of the documents?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Can this be blown up a little? I'm not -- unable to read everything very clearly. Yes, these are my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what you said a few minutes ago about filling in the chart, it being the truth, and those comments reflecting what you had to say about the documents, do you stick by that in relation to this document which you signed?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies. It was the wrong channel. The witness said: There's no reason why I shouldn't stick by what I said, namely that these are my comments and the documents I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this chart. If it could be MFI'd until certain issues are resolved between myself and Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Jordash is just asking it to be marked for identification, then obviously there's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the number -- could a number be assigned to this document to be marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be D336, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D336 is marked for identification, under seal. Madam Registrar, perhaps you could already anticipate for [Realtime transcript read in error "four"] numbers to be assigned to documents appearing in this chart which have not yet received exhibit numbers so that we know how many numbers to reserve. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, 1D5001.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know if this is correct or not, but in relation to the last exhibit number, I think we have skipped D333. I don't know if that that's correct or not, but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D333 is pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Look at the screen, Mr. Witness. Have you seen the map before? Are these the locations which you wish to discuss and have discussed in your statement and will discuss in your testimony in court?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: These are the places where I spent about four and a half months working.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just inquire as to whether Your Honours have a paper copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We received a paper copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I have been asked by the Prosecution to have you identify Novi Sad. Would you indicate, please, where Novi Sad is?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: We would need to move the map a little for me to find it. It's not here. Zrenjanin, Backi Jarak, Backi Petrovac, Becej. I can't see it. Give me a moment. Right. How come I can't find it? After Backi Jarak I should see Novi Sad, but it's not there. It's not on the map. There's Petrovaradin. Petrovaradin is a suburb of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why I brought it up, just because it's an important location that for some reason didn't print on this map. We agree with the witnesses that it's next to Petrovaradin. If he could perhaps just mark an S for Novi Sad by the location that he's just circled, then the map would be useful to everyone looking at his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So where we -- where the witness marked this document with the red circle, that's the area where we are supposed to find Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's our understanding, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I guess that the Chamber would have found Novi Sad anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure why it's missing, actually. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hadn't even noticed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's proceed. May I take it that you would only need a number to be assigned to the marked map, which contains all the information and, in addition to that, the red circle indicating where approximately to find Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number for this map would be ... as marked by the witness ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D341 is admitted into evidence. Although the red circle has now disappeared, I take it that, as marked, it is admitted into evidence. There is no need to have it under seal, I take it. Then, talking about admission of documents, Mr. Jordash, I earlier encouraged you to upload the pseudonym sheet. Now, the witness has told us that the information is accurate. The form, however, says something about the signature. I'm not urging you to have it signed, but if you use forms where a signature is expected to be put on the form, then perhaps for the future it would be better to really have that signature. But there's no doubt, I think, about, even without a signature, that the witness stated that the information is accurate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I'd like to take you through some of the evidence which is now before the Court and ask you to elaborate on some of it and clarify some of it. Bear in mind that the Court now has your statement and the corrections and the chart. Please could we have D334 on the screen. Could we go to page 3, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be preferable to have both the B/C/S and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the English? And not two times the English text. Yes, we have it now. Could we move to the right paragraph in B/C/S. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 6 you testify to the engagement of PJM units in 1991. "... engaged to assist because of an increased level of security risk." And in paragraph 7, you speak and elaborate about these PJM units. Are you able to describe the nature of their tasks, generally?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Within the provincial SUP, Secretariat for Internal Affairs at Vojvodina, there was also a specialised police unit at the time, and they would be engaged on an ad hoc basis depending on the assignment put before them. Their basic tasks were to keep law and order, especially during mass events such as football matches and rallies. Their second task was to provide VIP security for VIPs coming to Vojvodina. And from 1990 to 2000 we were engaged in Kosovo, especially the border area and the border area with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in which way were they specialised?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: They were not the special unit. They were not specially trained for any kind of operation. Those were members of the regular police, mainly young people who had completed training in various courses aged up to 35. They were drawn from police stations across the territory of Vojvodina, and that is how several such units were formed within the provincial SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear: When you say "within the provincial SUP," are we -- are you talking about the public security or the state security?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I can only speak to the sector of public security, because I never worked in state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the PJM units have anything to do, in terms of chain of command or reporting, to the DB of Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No, we were not under the command or in obligation to report to state security employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the basic structure of the provincial SUP, the Vojvodina provincial SUP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Unlike other republics, the Republic of Serbia had three secretariats, one for central Serbia, Serbia proper, and two for each of the autonomous provinces. As far as Vojvodina is concerned, it had a provincial SUP with its public and state security sectors, and each of them had a chain of command. There was six secretariats: Sombor, Apatin, Zrenjanin, Novi Sad, Mitrovica, and Subotica. If you want me to, I can explain the structure in greater detail within each secretariat. For instance, there were OUPs, organisational units, but I don't think it's relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've named, I think -- well, what's been picked up by translation, of the six secretariats we have Novi Sad, Mitrovica, Subotica. What were the other three secretariats of the Vojvodina SUP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Sombor, Subotica, Mitrovica, Pancevo, Zrenjanin, Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just briefly, what was the relationship between the Vojvodina SUP and the Serbian MUP in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: We had our own secretary of the provincial SUP, whereas the republic SUP had its own secretary at the level of the republic. But I can say we worked autonomously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the secretary was the top of the organisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. The provincial secretary headed the secretariat and had two under-secretaries, one in charge of public security, another in charge of state security. At that time, Markov was the name of the provincial secretary. Predrag Markov.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 7, you testified to the four PJM units being subordinated to Zavisic, who was the commander of the police station in Novi Sad and the commander of the four PJM units. Who did Zavisic report to? Who -- what was the hierarchy above him?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: At that time, Zavisic was commander of the police station in Novi Sad, in charge of duty service and interventions. Within the PJP, he was company commander. And he commanded a unit that covered the sector from Mitrovica to Apatin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who did he report to? Let me try to shortcut this. In paragraph 8, you note that Zavisic was reporting to a department within the public security service and he was answerable to the head of the public security of the PSUP, Vojvodina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I can see that passage. As far as reporting is concerned, within the provincial SUP there was a department for the PJP, and the detachment commander was Momo Stojanovic, and there were also Stanoje Milanovic, Marinko Kresoja, and a large number of officers from the provincial SUP were part of that leadership. I understand I need to speak more slowly for the court reporter and the interpreters. That means that Zavisic reported to the people that I just enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 9, you testify to being the commander of the police station up until May of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. Before I joined the PJP, I worked in the intermunicipal secretariat OUP Srbobran and OUP Becej, and I was stationed in the police station in Becej.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to the beginning of 1991, before joining the PJM, did you notice any change in the type of work you were doing as a result of the breakout of conflict or violence in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As far as my area in Becej is concerned, it was relatively quiet and peaceful, because Becej has a population of 60 per cent Hungarians and 40 per cent others. I was born in Croatia, and most of my family from both the paternal and maternal sides were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash one of your previous questions was to whom did Zavisic report; what was the hierarchy above him. In the answer, mention is made of PJP, and you later repeated that question, but PJP here doesn't appear in one of these paragraphs, and I would like to know exactly what the acronym stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- unless it's a mistake, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you clarify, Mr. Witness: First of all, is there a difference between PJM and PJP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: There is no difference. For a while, we were PJM, standing for Posebna Jedinica Milicija, milicija being the old name for police. That's why the acronym changed from PJM to PJP. So perhaps it was just a slip of the tongue when looking at these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you recall when the acronym changed? Approximately which year?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you the year. But I believe that was the milestone year, between 1991 and 1993, when all the changes occurred. 1992, I think. I think 1992 is when the acronym changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 12. And you testify to being tasked to protect the area from Backa Palanka to Apatin. How many people were tasked with you to protect that area and what kind of distance did you cover?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Sometime around 12 May 1991, I and members of a part of the units from Srbobran and Becej were invited to report to OUP Odzaci that belonged to SUP Sombor where we were met by four officers of my rank and four other officers, Momo, Kresoje, Mr. Stojanovic, and Mr. Zavisic, where we were given our assignments and were told what our objective was, because the Croatian paramilitary units and MUP units had already crossed over into the territory of Serbia and they were carrying out illegal arrests, taking away and mistreating Serbian citizens. After receiving our assignments, we were assigned between Backa Palanka and Apatin, in three units. I was in Vajska; Nikolic was in Apatin; and another colleague from Pancevo was stationed in another location, so we covered that border with about 70 to 90 members of the PJM.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was your basic objectives and your basic tasks?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Considering that a large number of refugees had already arrived from Croatia into Serbia, moving mostly in boats that could hold four to five people, and there were already unrests and anxiety among citizenry along this invisible border between Serbia and Croatia, and there were many volunteers who were in that area helping out those people and some clashes had already occurred between paramilitary units on both sides, our objective was to calm down the situation, to receive all the fleeing people, and to remove people who were in possession of weapons illegally and legally, and to calm down the people, because the local police force had already lost control over the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there a particular ethnicity who -- who were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: From the time I came, people of various ethnicities were crossing over, Croatians and Hungarians and Ruthenians, because that crossing from Backa Palanka and Apatin is an area where the population is mixed. There were Serbians and Croatians and Hungarians. Practically all ethnicities were represented. And even the composition of my unit was very mixed. There were Hungarians, Serbs, Croatians, Ruthenians. We never discriminated. We helped out all the people who were coming our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of assistance did you provide to those who were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The first thing we did was regarding the boats, because the boats were handled by skippers who were not trained. We asked them not to take in too many people per boat, and we admitted all these incoming people and turned them over to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In paragraph 14, you testify to a situation at the Danube, and you note that your PJM platoon controlled the direction Backa Palanka, Sombor, and the check-point Vajska. How big was the check-point at Vajska, what kind of check-point was it, how far from the Danube, and how many people were manning it?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: From Backa Palanka to Apatin, the population could not cross the river across the bridges because they were controlled by the Croatian paramilitary formations. People from Vukovar and the surrounding villages as well as from Backa Palanka, Becej, and all the other villages up to Apatin who had land across the river and family there tended to cross the river in boats. There were a few crossings there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I think your question was: "How big was the check-point at Vajska, how far was it from the Danube, and how many people were manning it." That is, about the check-point. Your answer is focussing on why people want to cross or whether they could cross or not. Could you please focus your answer on the question. First question: How big was the check-point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The check-point was about 10 square metres big. There were three check-points in that position and a group of 25 to 30 members of the PJP was assigned to control those three crossings and the stretch from Backa Palanka to Odzaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how far was it from the Danube? Or was it at the Danube river.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each of those crossings was on the Danube river itself. The first one, the so-called Rakic Ovsalas [phoen], was across the river from Vukovar. The second one was across the river from Borovo Naselje. And the third one was across the river from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there any reason why check-points were put at those locations rather than at other places along the Danube?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Those had been legal crosses -- crossings even before. This is where the bank was conducive to crossing. But when we arrived, the population wanted to cross elsewhere and that's why they set up illegal crossings. With the few people that we had, we tried to control those illegal crosses by way of setting up patrols and to direct the population to the three legal crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, a moment or two ago you noted that "From Backa Palanka to Apatin, the population could not cross the river across the bridges because they were controlled by the Croatian paramilitary formations." First of all, who were the Croatian paramilitary formations? What kind of organisations were they? What were they constituted of -- or who were they constituted of?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: At that time, I knew very little about them. However, when I arrived at the crossing, I learned a lot. They were criminals who had been armed by the legal institutions of the Republic of Croatia. They wanted Croatia to secede from the former Yugoslavia, or the then-Yugoslavia, as it were. I couldn't understand that because I worked in a state institution and I had been brought up to believe that arms can be carried only by the -- by those who had a licence to carry arms, and that means the police and the military and a few individuals who had a special permit to carry arms, given to them by the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what were these criminals doing to prevent people from crossing the bridges?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Every citizen who was not of Croatian ethnicity was ill-treated. His personal effects were seized, money, jewellery. And if they were travelling in a good passenger vehicle, that was confiscated as well. That is why people resorted to other means of crossings. Meaning barges and boats. This was a riskier way to cross but at least they managed to keep their personal effects. I can say that at the time in the territory of the Republic of Croatia people used false IDs, or, rather, IDs were undergoing changes, and that people of Serbian ethnicity had different last -- digits on their IDs to make sure that everybody knew that they were Serbs, that they were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long -- are you able to put a time on this? How long were the Croatian paramilitaries in control of the bridges in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The bridge in Backa Palanka was closed and mined, so it couldn't be used at all. And the bridge near Dalj could not be used before Dalj was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And are you -- do you know when that was, when Dalj was liberated?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: In 1991, on the 2nd of August. But, really, I'm trying to provide you with as much information as possible. I'm trying to retrieve all that information from my long-term memory. So I may be mistaken on some names and dates. Please do not hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's okay. If you don't remember, you don't remember. It's a long time ago. Paragraph 13 of your statement, you make mention of an incident when members of the ZNG entered the territory of Vojvodina, and you testified to the control of the check-points being intensified. In which way were the check-points intensified at this point in time, following this incident?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: After that incident, we arrived in the area that I described in my statement. One of the reasons or pretexts, as it were, was the fact that a group of ZNGs crossed over to the territory of Serbia. They captured a number of fishermen and women, they ill-treated them, and then released them. After a report was filed by those individuals, we were sent to that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were there any incidents in Apatin when you were tasked to protect that area in 1991, or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: At that time, ZNGs crossed one more time. They were masked in military uniforms, and they crossed over to the territory of Serbia in military vehicles. They wreaked havoc there. The police had to intervene, and a number of people were arrested and their further intentions were thus thwarted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly or approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: That was probably in 1991. In late 1991 or early 1992. Again, I'm not sure about the year. I know that there were two incidents, and I've just described the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know which police had to intervene and make the arrests?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Our forces tried to arrest them, but they were not trained for such tasks. Therefore, the military had to intervene and carry out the task. I know that Radovan Stojcic, also known as Badza, was involved in that mission. But he couldn't do anything because they were in armoured vehicles and we didn't have any tools or weapons to carry out such a demanding task.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to paragraph 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There, you testify to the conflict starting and the situation changing "with the PJM being sent to the border to protect the entering of people with weapons." Could you explain what this change meant?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: When I arrived on the 15th of May and when I joined men at the check-point, I found a group of civilians there. They were armed with hunting rifles and carbines. And since I'm a man who understand people and I don't lose my temper easily, I tried to reason with them. I told them that there was no need for them to be there. I told them that I represented the state and that nobody else should be there but me, especially if they were carrying arms. Jovo Ostojic was also there with two or three men of his. He reacted vehemently because he --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I was just asking -- I'm going to come to the man you've just mentioned shortly. But could I just ask you, first of all: What were your tasks and how did they change, as indicated in paragraph 17. You note there that: "Once the conflict started, the situation changed, with the PJM being sent to the border to protect the entering of people with weapons." Was that a change from when the usual tasks of the PJM that you've been talking about up till now?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. Changes did happen. An armed conflict had already broken out in Borovo. Arms were being used and there were casualties. PJMs had had to remove anybody who was moving about illegally, and especially those who were carrying hunting rifles, for which they had appropriate licences from the regional organs. We did that to provide for the security of members of the police and the citizens who were crossing the river there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time, and I wondered if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash, I think it's a convenient moment. If you would allow me, because it might be difficult to get back to that after the break. You said that you couldn't arrest those who had entered Serbia and that the intervention of the army was needed. Where were they finally arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those individuals who were in the area from the moment we arrived were arrested. Either they crossed from Croatia or from Serbia. If they had arms, they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't answer my question, really. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I think Your Honour may be at odds with the witness. I think the witness doesn't appreciate you're talking about Apatin, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to go back to the transcript. One second, please. Yes, you told us - and I'll take you back to the relevant part of your evidence - you said that there were two incidents. You had described the second of these incidents. You were then asked: "And do you know which police had to intervene and make the arrests?" You said: "Our forces tried to arrest them, but they were not trained for such tasks. Therefore, the military had to intervene and carry out the task." Which I understand to be the task of arresting those persons. You said Badza was involved in that mission. He couldn't do anything because they had armoured vehicles. Now, finally: Were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After a day and a half, they were arrested by the JNA. So it was on the second day of their stay in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where was that? Was that on the Vojvodina territory or was it in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apatin is in Vojvodina, which means that it was in the territory of Serbia. Or, in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's where they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what then happened to them? Were they brought to court or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A group of them were tried. But as far as I know, eventually they were exchanged for the members of the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let's take a break first. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two brief matters before we continue. An e-mail was sent by the Prosecution in relation to the protective measures. Mr. Groome, first of all, I would like to put that on the record, that you do oppose finally to grant the protective measures. There's a bit of a dilemma for us. We have not finally decided. The request was there. You have responded to that request. We have not yet asked, for this specific witness, further details from the Government of Serbia and I might have overlooked that. If you go not far enough, then you're in trouble, if you want to grant the request as a whole. If you go too far, not in every respect, the redaction of the protection can be achieved. So therefore this is a bit of a dilemma there. The Chamber is aware of it. We have proceeded in the past in a similar way. I do understand the objections raised by the Prosecution. This is on the record, unless you would like to add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I appreciate the difficult circumstances of such a situation and appreciate that the Chamber considered it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Groome. Then, finally, I may not have pronounced well, when I asked Madam Registrar to anticipate for assigning numbers, or for reserving numbers, whether I said "for," f-o-r, or f-o-u-r, as it appears in the transcript. I blame my own pronunciation for that. However, Madam Registrar has followed the transcript, where far more numbers needed to be reserved, which results in the following. Madam Registrar, have you a suggestion how to resolve it; could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will re-assign a number that was assigned to a document ID 5001 marked by the witness in court, which received number D341. We receive instead number D337 and numbers -- so number D341 will be vacated. And instead I will later on file a chart with the pre-assigned exhibit numbers for 26 documents without an exhibit number assigned in the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I'll seek some additional training in properly pronouncing the difference between "for" and "four." D341 is vacated and will be most likely in the range of pre-assigned numbers for 26 documents. And then in order to avoid further confusion, Madam Registrar, instead you -- of D341, you would assign what number to what is, until now, D341?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number would be D337, for the map marked in court by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised, because we ended up at D341 after we had used the previous numbers, isn't it? Including D337, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The last number that was assigned to the chart was D336, and then I reserved four numbers, and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point. So from the four reserved numbers, now we used the first one, which is D337, for the map marked by the witness. So D337 now is a map marked by the witness; and the following 26 numbers then are reserved, and we'll find that on your chart to be produced soon. That is clear. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could we have a look at paragraph 25 of your statement, please. At paragraph 25 you discuss your first day of work and a man called Jovo Ostojic and an incident where he tried to go through the crossing with arms. Who was Jovo Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Jovo Ostojic was a resident of Serbia. He resided in Prigravica. He was a man who belonged to either the Serbian Chetnik movement or to some other political option. A man who used to wear a leather jacket. He sported a beard. He had long hair, bulging eyes. He looked terrifying to me when he came out of the woods. But I'm not easily intimidated. I stood in front of him. I had a conversation to him, and I made him aware who the boss was in the area. He was quite displeased, and he --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He told you that he was involved in the organisation of acceptance of refugees. Did you accept that; and, if not, what did you learn, if anything, about what he in fact wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I'm sure that he did work on the reception of civilians quite a lot. The civilians had started arriving from the 1st of May. I myself arrived on the 13th of May. However, when I arrived, I didn't want anybody else to be involved in that but me. I was the only representative of the state, and I was the only one in a position to be involved in that. He protested but he left. I did not disarm him because that was my first encounter with him. If he had been impertinent after that or if he had disobeyed, I'm sure that I would have disarmed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He "returned on several occasions to cross the border but then he came more polite and came unarmed." Do you know why he was crossing the border?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: After that, on several occasions he did arrive. But having realized who was the boss, he was polite, well-mannered, and I allowed him to cross because he had relatives in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 29, you speak about Seselj crossing the point as an unarmed citizen. Did Seselj ever cross as an armed citizen?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I've already said that I'm telling the truth, and I said it in my statement that he did cross on several occasions. He attended Soskocanin's burial. He was always unarmed. And he was escorted by two or three men who also didn't carry any arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, P1344.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a speech that -- or, sorry, an interview, an excerpt from an interview that Seselj gave, I think, in 1991 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 4 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just to confirm, you've seen this interview before, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, the section I'm interested in begins with Seselj saying this: "There are no troops from Serbia or from Montenegro. That is a fact. However, there are volunteers who have come to fight for the liberty of the Serbian people, and no one can prevent them from coming. We had a lot of problems, you know. Everything was much easier during the war for Srpska Krajina. Then, at first, we had to smuggle volunteers across the Danube to Slavonia. We feared the Serbian police and the Yugoslav Army more than we feared the Ustashas as we smuggled them across the Danube. And then, when the war broke out with full intensity, then we cooperated fully with the army." Do you accept or do you agree with what Mr. Seselj said then about his fear of the Serbian police and his having to smuggling Serbian volunteers across the Danube?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I had orders that nobody is to be allowed to cross over to the other side carrying weapons, and I obeyed that order in full. Which means that he was not able to cross. And if he did, it could have been only in areas where I had no control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware if any of your colleagues on the other check-points had the same objectives as yourself and whether, in fact, they sought to achieve those objectives?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: All four senior officers received the same orders, the same assignments, and I can say that there's no reason for me to believe that these orders were not followed, knowing well the colleagues who were working with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Seselj then goes on to say, in relation to cooperating fully with the army at a later stage: "And in agreement with the army, we sent volunteers. We even had some barracks, depots, uniforms, and so forth at our disposal." Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I know after I returned to Becej from that area the Yugoslav People's Army providing barracks in Belgrade where volunteers gathered and were sent from there, unarmed and organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you encounter these men at the check-points?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No. In my time, even if they had come, they would not have been able to cross. Because approval was required for crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to identify when that changed, when it was that Seselj's Men were travelling, as you've said, organised and unarmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I have on the screen, please, 1D01950. I beg your pardon. It's D291, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, what you're going to see, Mr. Witness, is a State Security Service for Belgrade report, dated 15th of July, 1991. Please have a read through.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: "The State Security Administration for Belgrade, 3rd Department, Official Note --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I didn't mean for you to read it aloud. Just read the document to yourself, just to familiarize yourself with the contents. Then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Sorry. I have read this Official Note several times before, so you can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 1, I want to ask you about the reference to Pekic. Page one of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S. And the Official Note, as we can see, discusses the gathering of volunteers by the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik movement. And towards the bottom of the page, it's noted that retired General Dusan Pekic and Dragoljub Bulat were involved in the way described. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As I arrived at the crossing to Vajska, I heard the names of Jovic and Pekic and all these people. I know that Mirko Jovic had a few members in Borovo Selo before he arrived. I got this information from the locals and I passed it on to my superiors. And even during my time at the crossing the retired general was mentioned as having crossed over, not at my crossing, but it was said that he had been in Borovo Selo, Dalj, and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was it said what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No, no. Even if he had been active, it must have been in concert with the Yugoslav People's Army because all the retired staff, all the retired personnel, were still in contact with the army. I don't know that man personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 2, please, of the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The report, or the Official Note, states: "According to our intelligence, besides ... Petkovic and Rankic from the SRS, Bulat and Ciganovic [phoen] also participate in the direct transfer of the volunteers to the Slavonia and the SAO of Krajina. Thus, on the 8th of July, 1991, they organised a ferry crossing on the Danube for a group of volunteers being sent to Borovo Selo." Did you ever learn about these men and their involvement in the direct transfer of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I know that Jovo was trying, because we met a couple of times, to persuade me to let a certain group through, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say "Jovo," are you referring to the Jovan Ostojic we see in the paragraph there?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes, I mean him. The one who was mentioned in the paragraph. He didn't come with that group. The information that I had was that he had a certain number of volunteers who wanted to cross over. I told him that was not on, and I did not make it possible for that group to cross, because for every group that was to be let through, there had to be a written approval signed by superior authorities. Only two such approvals were received during my tenure in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, going to page 3 of the B/C/S but page 2 of the English, I just want to ask you about a training ground referred to here. The paragraph I'm interested in starts with: "The entire action of sending volunteers was reorganised after this. It was decided that this would be led by Petkovic from his apartment and not from the SRS premises, together with Bulat. It was also decided that until a suitable training ground was found near Belgrade the volunteers would be sent to the training ground in Prigravica, where they would be given equipment and weapons and undergo brief training. According to Ostojic, the training ground in Prigravica was fully equipped to take in 200 or 300 volunteers for training and send them to Slavonian villages. A troop review of the volunteers of the Serbian army was scheduled for 1900 hours on the 13th of July, 1991, in this training ground, but it was postponed and only a rally was held." Do you know anything about this training ground and the facts or references made here in this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Since I disallowed these volunteers to cross, they were with Jovo Ostojic in Prigravica where they spent a couple of days trying to find training grounds. But in the meantime, Jovo Ostojic, untrained as he was, inflicted an injury upon himself while handling a weapon, and that's how it all ended. It never came to anything. Also, a criminal complaint was filed against Jovo Ostojic for all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Prigravica, did it become a training ground at any point?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 32 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please -- one second. 1D5000, please. D334.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You're referring here in paragraph 32, Mr. Witness, to viewing a permit signed by Bogdanovic. And you testify that: "Only people with a permit from the highest level would be allowed to cross the border with a weapon. This was a permit signed by Bogdanovic or the secretariat of the Vojvodina MUP, Markov." Who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I got that order from Zavisic and the superior officers who had sent me from my police station in Odzaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if that order was an order which was in place at your check-point or all the check-points?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: When we were receiving our assignments, all the officers were present. That means that order applied to all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know how long that order was in place?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: For the duration of my engagement on that assignment, the order was not changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could I seek some clarification of one of the previous answers. Witness, you were asked whether Prigravica did become a training ground at any point. And then you said: "As far as I know, no." Do you have any specific knowledge which would allow you to more positively say that it did not become a training ground; or is it that you just never heard about it to ever have become a training ground? So is there any specific knowledge which allows you either to more positively say it never was a training ground; or is it that you just do not have any information? Because the report that was just put to you is, to some extent, detailed. It says it was fully equipped; it would take 200 or 300 men; people were sent from there to Slavonia; there was something scheduled for the 13th of July, which finally did not take place. So there are quite a lot of details. My question to you is - where you say not to your knowledge it ever became a training ground - what is the basis specifically for that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I knew Jovo Ostojic and the people around him. I know he was a man from Prigravica, and he was the one who would have organised all that. But after he wounded himself, his close associates came by the crossing, by the check-point, several times, and I heard from them that the idea never came through. And I know from a colleague who worked at another check-point that SUP Sombor did its job. All the weapons and everything found in the house of Jovo Ostojic and his friends was confiscated, and a criminal complaint was filed against all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that there was a concentration, then, of weapons in or around his -- in -- in his house and that those weapons were confiscated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm addressing the parties. Is there anything known about the criminal complaint filed against Mr. Ostojic in this respect which would shed additional light on what exactly was found? Was it just weapons in a house; or was it, as the report seems to suggest, that there was a training grounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, no. But we can do some research into the exhibit, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such evidence, Your Honour, but I will ask that it be investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please report to the Chamber at the earliest possibility. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Witness, to have a look at P18.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is another speech or interview with Seselj somewhat later; I think 1993 or 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we could have page 14 of the B/C/S and 14 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just to confirm: You've seen this before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to see if you can shed any light on some of the remarks made by Seselj. He's asked the question: "Can we briefly, since you were not in Borovo Selo, and in principle, we are working for somebody who was in touch, can you explain once more regarding Bogdanovic? He was not, he was -- he was not officially ... actually, he was sacked and reinstated again." And then going over the page in the B/C/S: "No, he wasn't sacked. He was replaced from the position of minister. That is, he was made to submit his resignation. However, his resignation only had a formal significance. In essence, he remained the main police chief in Serbia, and he is still the key police figure, because Sokolovic mainly doesn't interfere in every affair, and the domestic public knows it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. "I had my first contact with Bogdanovic in July 1991. Until then, the contacts went through Vukasin Soskocanin. He was later found dead under very suspicious circumstances. They say that he had drowned in the Danube. We were suspicious about it, and there are indications that he was executed due to certain matters that were never cleared."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So, first question: Do you know anything about the drowning of Soskocanin?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I'd heard stories about Vukasin Soskocanin when I came to the check-point. And a couple of days into my stint, Petar Licanin handed him over to me personally. Petar Licanin is the man who found him in the Danube. After that, Soskocanin was brought to the territory of Vojvodina, where a team of prosecutors and forensic experts did their job on the body and then they -- it was turned over to the family for burial. I cannot say anything about Soskocanin because I never met him. I only saw him when he was dead, that one time. But I can say that the residents of Borovo Selo and others had a lot of praise for the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, reading on, Seselj says that: "My first meeting with Bogdanovic took place in July 1991 when I was elected deputy in the national assembly and we met at the Serbian Assembly. We really didn't have any contact before that." Going over the page, to page 15 of the English: "However, we established a close relationship and met often." Were you aware of any relationship between Bogdanovic and Seselj? Is that something that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I worked in the Ministry of Interior. I was on assignment. I was never a politician. Politics never interested me, and I'm not interested in those interrelations. I know Radmilo Bogdanovic because he was the secretary for internal affairs for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me read on a bit, to page 16 of the B/C/S and page 15 of the English. Seselj says that: "We regained [sic] this trust very quickly and then the regime also put the army barracks in Bubanj Potok at our disposal. An entire army barracks was provided only for the Serbian Radical Party's volunteers, and we were gathering our volunteers in Belgrade. Here we received uniforms and weapons for them, buses to take them to battle-fields, and so forth. This was very well organised." Do you go anything about that? Is that something you can comment on?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Regarding the Bubanj Potok barracks in Belgrade, it was not placed at the disposal of the Serbian Radical Party. What did happen was that all volunteers who reported, regardless of their political affiliation, reported there, and the army took them into their ranks. I don't know what Seselj is talking about. I'm telling you the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if there was any training there?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask, please, for you to look at P02990. Now, in the chart that you've completed - Your Honour, page 8 - you note: "I recognise the signature. This is the same signature that was included on the permission, Arkan and Kostic." Could you just clarify which signature you recognise?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I recognise the signature on the left-hand side of the document, Radmilo Bogdanovic. This is a signature that I saw on the certificate at the crossings. I confiscated those two certificates, and I forwarded them to Zavisic with my report. Since I was rewarded by Radmilo Bogdanovic, I am quite familiar with this signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, what did you just say? Since you were, what, by Radmilo Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I was decorated as a member of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was that? And what was the decoration for?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: In 1990, I was decorated for my work and the results achieved in elucidating crimes and catching the perpetrators of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At the time when you met Arkan and he produced permission signed by Bogdanovic -- or perhaps just going back one step. At the time when Arkan insisted he had a relationship with Bogdanovic, had you been aware of that relationship prior to that moment?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: My first contact with Arkan was on that day. I stated that in my statement. I was an employee of a very small police station in a town that numbered 20.000 and the municipality had 40.000 inhabitants. I had never come in touch with criminals of that calibre. My first contact with him was as follows: He said, I am Arkan, and I replied, I am Bogunovic. He wanted to cross; I told him no. To which he jumped, started screaming and calling me names. However, I explained to him what he could do and then he said who he was sent by. And then I said: Okay, if you were certainty by him, let him give you a permission and sign it and then I will let you go. I didn't allow him to cross that night. He came back the following morning with a permission with an appropriate heading, all the names of the people were listed, as well as the number of vehicles, and then I allowed him to cross. There were the names of some five or six or perhaps seven people, but it doesn't really matter. What matters is the fact that he did cross but with an adequate permission. And I know that he went to Tenja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... try to understand the situation a bit more. This was July of 1991, as you've said in your statement. Did Arkan have a reputation at that point in time? Was he known to you by reputation or not?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I said that that was my first contact with him. Before that, I had never heard of Zeljko Raznjatovic, also known as Arkan. Once he crossed, I had a chat with my colleagues, policemen, and other people. I heard stories about him, but I had never been aware of those stories before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I was not interested in him. He was not a problem in my area. He was a problem in Belgrade, and it was up to the police in Belgrade to deal with him and to solve that problem. I carried my orders. I respected the law. I did not allow him to cross before he managed to obtain the necessary document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have your statement back on the screen, please. D334. And paragraph forty -- paragraph 41. And this is the subject of operatives of intelligence services crossing the border. Now, at your particular crossing, were there any permanent DB, whether from Vojvodina DB or the Serbian DB, stationed at your crossing? Let me rephrase that. I think it's a bit confused. At your particular crossing, were there any DB from either Vojvodina DB or the Serbian DB stationed on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: At the crossing where I served, as well as in the others, no members of the DB of either Vojvodina or Serbia were stationed. Members of the state security of Vojvodina did come to my crossing from time to time during the day. They were briefed either by me or my colleagues as to what was going on. Since we were all members of the Ministry of the Interior, we shared all the information with those people. None of them ever crossed the river, which means that no members of the DB from Serbia came to my check-point. They did come from Vojvodina. I gave you their names. I'm sure that there were others, but you have to understand that I can't remember all of their names at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How often would you see the operative Lemic?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Not that often as Glusica and Sarac. Lemic did not cross as many times as Glusica and Sarac, and two other members whose names I don't know. I know that they were members of the state security in Novi Sad. Until the moment I left the service, they were still affiliated with the state security of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear of Lemic doing anything other than collecting information?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: There was nothing for him to do at the crossing but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And away from the crossing, do you know if he did anything other than collect information?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: If he had done anything else, I suppose I would know. I had daily patrols. I set up daily ambushes. And we never noticed that man. All the vehicles of the regional SUP were known to us. They were of a newer make and not a common sight in the area. That's why we knew them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you ever able to form an opinion about the way in which Lemic acted as a professional in gathering information?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Whatever information DB officials received they received either from me or my colleagues or the persons who were being interviewed at the crossing at the time when they appeared. If they received any other information, they could receive it from other people in the depth of the territory. I did not see them talking to anybody else at the crossing more often than they did to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to Lazar Sarac, did you ever hear that he was involved in anything other than collecting information? Or did you see him involved in anything other than collecting information?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Lazar Sarac was a young operative, just like I was at the time. I don't think that he was capable of doing anything else but collecting information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what about Branko Glusica?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Branko Glusica was at the check-points every day, and he talked to me. He inspected the records that we kept at the check-points. Whatever information we had we conveyed to him. Moreover, I had an argument with the operative Glusica because we had information about some arms being kept at the farm of Mile Jerenkic and we wanted to seize those weapons as soon as possible. He actually conveyed that information to my superior, which is why I lost credibility with my informer, a person who helped me to make the area as secure as possible and as weapons-free as possible. That was my argument with Glusica about [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 46. And you, there, discuss a man called (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, may I remind you that the whole story about Arkan at the border, your whole examination hardly revealed anything what we could not yet read in the statement. Now, more or less, operatives of intelligence services crossing the border is approximately the same. Of course, there's some additional information. If he says they received information, they sought information, then you asked whether you -- he is aware of any other activity, then the witness says no. Of course, if it's not in his statement about other activities, we take it on the basis of the statement that that was what he knew about that person. I hope that we're not going on another area through the same repetitious exercise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why did you consider (redacted) to be unimportant? Why did you conclude he was doing nothing?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: He crossed quite often. His conduct and his manner of talking to us and the others made me conclude that he wasn't interested in anything but money. He wanted to do as little as possible and to be paid as much as possible at the same time. He always asked me about my salary, about my bonus for being there, whether I had any daily allowance, and things like that. That was the main thing on his mind: money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 48. And we're dealing now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 46 is approximately the same story as for the previous ones. Of course, that little details, that he would like to be paid for doing nothing and that, that's because he asked about daily allowances, et cetera, but it doesn't add, really, to the information unless there's any specific issue in relation to that which you would like to draw our attention to. But I have not heard any of that, although I asked you to avoid a similar thing as with Arkan crossing the border and the operatives crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please try to -- to provide new, relevant, focussed information if you further examine the witness on this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The problem is, Your Honour, that (redacted) is a man who has been raised by the Prosecution. We're not sure exactly why. But he has been attributed to the DB. And we're not sure what he's supposed to have done or why he is to be attributed to the accused. So we try to raise the details we can to deal with any possible allegation which we know is coming at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you should not have introduced the evidence which we find in paragraph 46. My issue is that giving details as "What showed that he was interested in money," which, of course, is now directly contradicting what the Prosecutor says, and is just, I would say, illustrative for what we find in paragraph 46. I'm not complaining about what we find in 46. What I'm complaining about is about asking questions and -- the same is true for the whole Arkan story. More than one page of transcript where there's hardly anything which we do not find yet in 33, 34, 35, 36, and it's -- don't misunderstand. I'm not saying that you're not raising relevant -- that you're raising irrelevant issues; I'm saying that it's repetitious to what we find already in the statement. And to the extent you give further details, it is so limited compared to what we find in the statement, that I wonder whether there are not more important questions to be put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
