utterances.text: At paragraph 48, Mr. Witness, you describe there being instructed by Badza to go to Eastern Slavonia. And you used the term that you were asked if you were willing to go as a volunteer. Why do you describe yourself as a volunteer in this circumstance?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic and Ilija Kojic insisted, as well as a number of citizens from Borovo Selo and surrounding villages, that I should cross over and help them after having seen the kind of discipline that had been instituted at the check-point and what we did. And then Badza and my superior Zavisic asked me if I was prepared to cross over as a volunteer, and then I said, I don't see why not. If necessary, I'll go. I was born in Croatia. Lots of my relatives were there in the area. I spoke to my parents on a daily basis. They complained how difficult it was for their relatives. That's why I agreed to cross over as a volunteer. Not as a member of the Ministry of Interior but, as all the other volunteers who had crossed over, with a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In paragraph 49 you describe that everybody continued to be paid by the MUP Serbia as if they were still working in their function in Serbia. For example, "I was paid by the OUP Becej, as the commander of the police." Was there a stated arrangement? Was there a meeting where this arrangement was discussed with members of the public security? That is, that you would go as a volunteer but continue to receive your salary.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No meeting took place at the ministry level. Badza and Zavisic were the only ones behind that, and they spoke to me. All the volunteers who crossed over were paid by their original companies, which means that I was paid by the ministry, which -- with which I was affiliated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At paragraph 60, you say: "We went to Eastern Slavonia together with Goran Hadzic, who decided that we would be based in Erdut." How do you know that it was Hadzic who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Hadzic was there waiting for us on the bridge. He escorted us to Erdut, to what then became the centre. Before that, it was an area where recruits had been trained. Us five officers and 16 members of the PJP were billeted there. And he told us what we would be doing, where and how. After that, we received all of our instructions from Radovan Stojcic, also known as Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You note in paragraph 50 that Badza addressed you and told you that you would be training members of the TO. What was the purpose of the training, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Since I had already worked at the crossing, I was aware of the situation and I knew that a lot of wounds were self-inflicted, that people lost their lives as a result of inability to handle arms. We knew that the first thing we had to do was to train members of the TO. In other words, the locals in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you about training at this point. When you arrived in Eastern Slavonia in August/September 1991, had any of the locals been trained?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As far as I know, there had been some attempts, several attempts, to train the local population, members of the TO of those settlements. But all those attempts failed, as far as I know. The first time something like that was organised, it involved a person who had been training in Golubic as a member of the famous Knindze. He tried to train them but he couldn't accomplish much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was his name, please?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, his family name was Radenkovic. I don't know what his first name was. I really don't know now. But if it's important, when I come back to Serbia I'll try to find his name and I will send it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say he tried to train, who had he tried to train and why hadn't he accomplished much?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: He tried to train the locals of all the villages. But he did not have the necessary authority to impose himself upon the members of the TO there. He simply did not display the necessary knowledge to train them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which areas had he tried to train members of the TO in?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: In Borovo Selo and the surrounding villages. All those villages are marked on the map that we saw at the beginning. Borovo Selo, Tenja, Erdut, Bobota. I'm sure that I will omit one or two. But we're talking about the villages in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So were you aware of any other attempts to train before you began your training?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: There were attempts on the part of various people, locals or reserve officers. The training never took off the ground. If anything had happened, the results were disappointing. It was very difficult for anybody to -- to impose themselves upon those people who were in such a situation, especially if those people didn't trust them. Then nothing could be done. People were simply afraid for their lives, their property, their children's lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you've -- you tell us at paragraph 53 that you trained locals from various settlements, including those marked on the map. Whilst you were training locals and the volunteers who came from Serbia, were you aware of anybody else conducting training in the region?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: When we crossed over, nobody else was involved in training. We were the only ones who had taken the task upon ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you come across a man called Baja?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: When I toured the area in order to obtain information from the military and everybody else to be able to accomplish my mission, and that was to mark all the units in the area on the map, starting with the military, the Territorial Defence, and others, I did come across a person called Milovac [phoen] who was a former member of the Novi Sad SUP. He was fired. His nickname was Baja. He sported a red beret. He bragged about some training that he conducted. However, knowing him, I'm sure that he did not have the necessary knowledge to do it. Even if he had been involved in training, I'm sure that his group was small and that the intention for them was not to defend the population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where did you claim to have conducted training?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think it was Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever meet a recruit from Ilok whilst you were in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Never. Nobody but him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to your training, what precise role, then, did you play? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Since I was the Chief of Staff, my role was to make a rota and inform members of the TO as to what would be done on what day and in what settlement. More specifically, I can tell you that each day a group of three or four members of the police who had crossed over together with us would go to one part of a settlement, for example, Borovo Selo. The first neighbourhood as you entered was Savola [phoen]. On that day, we conducted training or, rather, we stayed for three or for days, then we moved to Srepulje [phoen], and then we moved to the centre. It was just the basic infantry training, familiarization with the weapons, in most cases weapons that could no longer be used. Obsolete. We also trained them about moving around the area and the bit about defence. Those were the A, B, Cs that we could teach them within the scope of three days, and this is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And after you had finished training a particular individual, did you have a role in directing where they should then be stationed or who they should be subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: We conducted training in settled areas, which means that those men were members of the local TO and they stayed there. However, a couple of volunteers that we trained, who had crossed across the bridge in the centre, we are talking about 10 or 15 people, underwent a training of 10 to 15 days. If they were good. Because Badza's intention was to set up a unit that would be equipped with weapons and vehicles. They would have been a mobile unit. However, that never materialised. We did not have the resources. In other words, we never received either the vehicles or the weapons. We had requested all of that from the TO or, rather, from Goran Hadzic and Ilija Kojic. But nothing came out of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just ask you if you would look at 1D5001, the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, before we move to the next subject, I'm looking at the clock. This would be approximately the time we take another break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm happy to stop here, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to inform you that you used, net time, two hours and four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hope to finish within 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you -- we were discussing training, and you noted that your role was to make a rota and inform members of the TO as to what would be done, on what day, and in which settlement. When you used the word "settlement," what do you mean by that precisely?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The training of the Territorial Defence was conducted in every populated area. One populated area was divided, for instance, into three stages. The first stage is one day; the second stage, the next day; and the next stage in the third part of the populated area. Or, if it was a smaller place, it was all conducted in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, how -- how was it -- are we talking about towns and villages or regions? How were you dividing up the regions, in terms of developing a rota system?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Considering that there were just a few instructors, we were able to conduct training in four places. That means on one day it was conducted in Borovo Selo, to take that example, in Sevovi [phoen], the second in Srepoja [phoen], the third in another area, and the fourth group remained in the centre itself, in Erdut. That group underwent training in the town itself, in the village itself. Not on training ground, but the very place where the trainees lived. We did not hold any towns because not a single town was under the control of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, P61.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, P61, as you're going to see, Mr. Witness, is a transcript of part of the Kula award ceremony. You've read this transcript before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you were present at the award ceremony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I was present at the celebration of the anniversary of the unit in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now I'll come back to the ceremony in general shortly, but I want to just ask you to look at one part of the speech given by Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 11, please, of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simatovic says, amongst a number of things, that the unit of the DB was involved, as we can see at the top of the English page at line 3, in setting up 26 training camps for special police units of Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina. And he lists a number of places in the Serbian Krajina, and I want to ask you about three of them; Lezimir, Ilok, and Vukovar. Did you ever meet a recruit from Lezimir when you were present training TOs in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Not a single trainee came to our area, nor do I know that there were any training centres there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to Vukovar, did you have any information about any training being conducted in Vukovar around the time you were present in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that training in Vukovar was conducted in Petrova Gora barracks, and a military man nicknamed Kole was in charge of that training. And he was also a member of the staff when I transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A member of which staff?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The one headed by Mr. Badza, the staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you say he was a military man, did he have a military background before coming to the staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, D341.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to return briefly to the subject of Ilok and the subject of any training there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D337 now; it's changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, we can see Ilok to the left of Backa Palanka, a little outcrop of Croatia. Now, you were present - is this right? - up until -- let me be sure about this. When did you leave Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long were you working under Badza in Eastern Slavonia? When did you leave?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: After the liberation of Dalj, a couple of days after the liberation of Dalj, we crossed over, and I had spent two months in that area because I had some family problems. I was divorced from my wife, and I got custody of the children, had to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you leave before or after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Before the fall of Vukovar. I left a couple of days before Bogdanovci fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In order to get from Vukovar to -- no, let me ask this differently. In order to get from Borovo Selo to Ilok at the time when you were in Eastern Slavonia, what was the route you would take?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Considering that we were based in Erdut not Borovo Selo, but even when I was around Borovo Selo, I had to go to Backa Palanka to go to Ilok from Croatia. I couldn't go straight to Ilok. I had to go via Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So is this -- does this follow, then: If there was training in Ilok, the recruits would have to go through Serbia and back into Croatia to get to Erdut?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The -- when you were in Eastern Slavonia, what was the population of Ilok? What, in terms of ethnicity, was the population?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: It was a mixed population. There were more Croats than Serbs and others, and that is so to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever have any complaints from Croats about training by Serbs in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No. It's quite certain if training had been conducted there that people would have complained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to explain how big Ilok is? How long would it take to walk across Ilok.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Ilok is a small place with a population of about 1.000-plus, so that you would cross it rather quickly, depending on how fast you walk. But it's a small place. You couldn't do anything without being noticed. If anything had gone on, it involved a small number of people. I don't think that I, as a graduate of the academy, would have chosen that place for -- for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? You, as a graduate of the academy, wouldn't have chosen that place for training. What do you mean by that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Strategically it is not a suitable place, especially because it's a multi-ethnic community and it would cause tensions in that community. And there is no link with the places where the trainees would be going. That's my thinking, at least. That's why I wouldn't do it there. Because if the unit had been trained there, the time it would take them to go to Erdut, they could have reached Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever meet a recruit whilst you were in Eastern Slavonia who had been trained at Pajzos? You didn't get the question. Did you ever meet a recruit while you were in Eastern Slavonia who had been trained at Pajzos?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No, never. I don't even know where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return to your statement, please; D334, I hope. Yeah. And paragraph 58. And this paragraph, Mr. Witness, discusses the arrival of a group of 40 police officers under Veljko Bogunovic. And you say in paragraph 58 you were not involved in equipping the police stations and you don't know anything about that. But in relation to these 40 police officers, do you know what it is they did? Did they, in fact, set up police stations?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: At the staff, the person who was in charge of training people for police stations was Mr. Zavisic. Three or four days after we arrived, that group of policemen also arrived, and they were accommodated in Dalj, in the kindergarten building. Tarbuk, Knezevic, and Momcilo Radovic were their leaders. I know a couple of names, but I don't think they were that important. I have already mentioned the main people. I can say that they were the ones who went to populated areas. And in areas where the police had their bases, they started training and equipping police stations. I can say that there were Tarbuk, Knezevic, Radovic, Boro Preradovic, and others, and in those places it worked. But in places where Veljko Bogunovic was in charge, it went rather sloppily, and that's why Badza often tried to remove him from that position and replace him. And if you want more details, I can provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know where Knezevic was?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Knezevic, I think, was in Ilok, and that was one of the better police stations that really started operating. From the information I have, all the houses and all the population were registered. It was an exemplary station. And Badza often praised him for the way he did his job, the way we were trained to do it, the way we were used to doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you in say places where Veljko Bogunovic was it was rather sloppy and Badza tried to remove him, why did Badza try to remove him, precisely?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Every job that he was given to do, he would not complete. And nothing ever worked that he handled, in the police stations that were assigned to him. Somebody else always had to come subsequently and do the job properly. And I don't know if I mentioned this before, but that group that arrived consisted of policemen that before the conflict had been members of the Croatian MUP and they had all come as volunteers to help form those units and to help lead these units. When I say "units," I mean police stations. I'm sorry, I suddenly moved to military terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, were these police officers and police stations involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just briefly, then we can move on: What were they involved in?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Their main job was to maintain law and order and normal life, to put a stop to looting and theft and looting from abandoned houses, and to take care of the property of all the Serbs and Croats who had abandoned their homes so that people could feel safe and return to their homes so that normal life could be restored to all these places. They were doing regular police work, and we all know what regular police work is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know where they received supplies from?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As far as uniforms are concerned, they brought their own uniforms. We from the staff did not procure uniforms, and I don't know where they were supplied from. We did write up lists of requirements, both for the Territorial Defence and the police, and we sent these to Badza. And where he forwarded these requests, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to paragraph 63 of your statement, a paragraph where you discuss Arkan. And you say: "Arkan and his unit were not under the command of the TO staff." Do you know who Arkan was subordinated to, if anybody, when on military operations?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I explained to what extent I knew Arkan. We had clashes with him all the time. Both we in the staff, excepting Badza, and the members of the police who came with us. He was involved in operations together with the JNA. But he always acted autonomously. He was not subordinated to anyone in the JNA. He would receive his own axis of movement, and he acted independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say "we had clashes with him all the time," who had clashes with him and what were the clashes about?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Arkan was a man who exploded very easily with a bad temper, aggressive, and, above all, he was a criminal. The people, the policemen from Belgrade knew that, and he didn't want to be in the same centre as him. And we senior officers suggested that to Badza and insisted, and we moved away from Erdut because we didn't want to be there because Arkan was in charge of security of the training centre itself. He was friends with Goran Hadzic, and he met with him quite often, and I suppose that he is the man to whom Arkan was subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to observe Arkan's relationship with Ilija Kojic?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I know Ilija Kojic rather well, and I did not see him often in the company of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if Ilija Kojic had formed a view about Arkan?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: His opinion was no different from mine or the opinion of all the policemen who were there. It was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I spoke to Ilija Kojic quite often and he told me that directly. And if he had had any power, it's certain that Arkan would not have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you say that? What did Kojic to say to give you that impression or have you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The entire population of that area was dissatisfied with the presence of Arkan because he acted very arrogantly and never respected any decisions that had been taken. In terms of deadlines and methods of work, he did as he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But what makes you think or conclude that Ilija Kojic would have removed Arkan if he'd had the power? What did Kojic say to you or anyone else that led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Well, considering that I was the one who had had contacts with Ilija Kojic at the check-point even before when he was crossing with Goran. He told me that he had asked Goran, that Arkan should leave the area. However, that didn't happen while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now just finally, just two brief subjects. I want to return to the Kula awards ceremony. Yesterday you watched a video, D131 in this case, which was part of the Kula awards ceremony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the video that you watched, D131, did it contain the whole of the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No, not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did it show and what was missed out?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The granting of awards to individuals was shown. However, decorations were handed out by politicians to members of the unit, members of the public security, members of the state security, members of the political circle, and prominent businessmen who had helped build the centre was left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you observe Kurtez [phoen] receiving an award?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was shown in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know why Kurtez received an award?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: For his contribution to the building of that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The man who was director of the customs administration at the time, Kurtez, gave a significant financial contribution to the building of that centre. I know that from my friends who knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In which capacity were you invited to the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: At the time, I was chief and also contributed to the building of that centre, and members of that unit came to Becej for -- to be trained in swimming.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Members of which unit?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: From the centre in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you receive an award?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: It's a bit personal but it's not a problem, I'll answer. I've told the truth all the way. The man who decided who would be given awards in the public security sector, when the name of Bogunovic was mentioned, he associated it with Veljko and that made him strike out my name, and I can also say that I am very sorry I did not receive an award from Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, who struck out your name and who associated Bogunovic, you, with Bogunovic, Veljko?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that. Badza had a lot of trouble with Veljko Bogunovic. And as soon as that last name was mentioned, I suffered the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did other people of the public security receive an award at the ceremony, and, if so, who made that decision to give them awards?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes, yes, some people did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who made the decision?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: The chief of public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, on the video there are some men who are referred to as veterans. What was your understanding of that term?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I saw those people as people who had fought at the various fronts for the unit to take off the ground and to continue existing in view of the fact that in Serbia, Kosovo, and Vojvodina special operations units already existed. I believed that the state did not have resources to finance another unit. I believed that that was just bragging in order to provide funds for this unit to continue working and for the other one to be disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just try to break that down a bit. Who were the veterans at that awards ceremony, as you understood them to be?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I know most of the veterans. They hail from different regions of the former Yugoslavia. That means that they were not all in the same place. That group consisted of people who had served in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When, as you understood it, did the state security unit, the JSO, or any state security unit come into --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Farr's on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And usually we wait until the question has been finished, unless there's any reason to intervene at any early stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll wait for the question to be finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please complete your question. Before you answer the question, would you please wait a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me try to break down what I was going to ask you, Mr. Witness. In the awards ceremony, Mr. Simatovic made a claim that there was a state security unit from 1991. What's your understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The objection is to foundation, Your Honour. There's been no evidence based on which the witness could reach a conclusion on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know. It may be part of his answer. Let's just ... Witness, when Mr. Simatovic made a claim that there was a state security unit from 1991, could you give us any information about the existence and the date mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, that unit had been established a year before that celebration and the award ceremony. I had participated in the building of that centre. And since my parents lived very near Kula, when I went there, when I visited there, I could see that refugees were housed in a very derelict building. There was no unit. I am not aware of any such unit having been formed either in Vojvodina, in Serbia, save for special units that belonged to the public security. There were three of them. One in Pristina, one in Belgrade, and one in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say as far as I know that unit had been established a year before the celebration. In your explanation, you very much refer to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... centre. And, of course, a centre is not the same as a unit. As far as the unit is concerned, your answer is that you were not aware of any such unit having been formed in -- either in Vojvodina, and then you talk that you do not know of any such unit being formed. Do you have any further factual information about the establishment of that unit, which you believe was established a year before the celebration, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any other information. For a unit to exist, it had to have a base, a seat, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be any base. Would you agree with that? Not necessarily the one you had on your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. However, that unit had 500 members who required a lot of space. They could not have been billeted in a small place, and they would have been really difficult to hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this is logic rather than factual information. Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock. You certainly went beyond your 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I can just take another five, then I can wrap up, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'm also keeping in the back of my mind what I said before about repetitiousness. But take your five minutes, but I'll be strict on that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to paragraph 67 of your statement. Jovica Stanisic and the arrest of Erdemovic. During this process of arresting Erdemovic and sending him to The Hague, did you speak directly to Mr. Stanisic or receive instructions or directions or orders indirectly from him?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Erdemovic and Kremenovic were arrested in the territory where I was the chief of the OUP. In the afternoon, I was called by a DB operative who was affiliated with the DB Novi Sad and he said that he had guests from the security centre, from the MUP. When they entered my office, I received the deputy chief of the centre in Novi Sad. I've been here for three days and I have been trying to remember his family name. He was at the celebration in the centre, but I can't remember his name. There was also Operative Blisin [phoen] and two members from Belgrade. They arrived and they told me that Stanisic sent his greetings and that he wanted us to carry the mission through to the end and that Stanisic said that those two men had to be sent to The Hague. He sent us a message that we had locate them. That activity lasted two days. And every evening when they returned to my office, they repeated that Jovica insisted that the two had to be sent to The Hague to be tried for what they had done, both the two of them as well as all the others who had been involved in similar things. At the end of the day, that operation was carried through successfully, owing to Jovica. They were sent to The Hague, and I hope that they are serving their sentences that they deserve. The only thing that I'm not sure about as I sit here today is whether one of them was Franko Simatovic who arrived or perhaps it was Mr. Tepavcevic. They look more or less the same and I didn't know any of them, so I would be mistaken to claim that it was either of them. Maybe one of the two of them could tell you which one came to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Kremenovic sent to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, during your time in contributing to this arrest and transfer, did you understand what it was that was motivating Stanisic to send these men to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As far as I know Stanisic, he respects the law, he's honest, and I believe that anybody who transgressed would be apprehended by him. Why not the Erdemovic and the other one? What they did was certainly not honest, and they deserve what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where do you -- sorry. Let me start that again. How did you form this opinion of Mr. Stanisic? What -- can you give us some facts to indicate where you came to that view.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I had a couple of tasks that I carried out in Belgrade. At that time, Jovica was still an operative and we worked together. I have a very high opinion of him and Mr. Stanisic's professional attitude to every task he was given. I hope that he, indeed, carried out all the tasks that were given to him successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he make reference to war crimes at any stage during the arrest of Erdemovic or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I was not at one celebration where Mr. Stanisic was present. I attended a lot of ceremonies at the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade, because I received awards and decorations. Mr. Stanisic was always there. And in every conversation he insisted and repeated that everybody who committed crimes had to face justice for what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I would be strict. The five minutes are over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Do we have a time indication, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try to finish before 7.00 today. If not, maybe I will need another ten minutes tomorrow, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. DST-074.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief conducted by my learned friend Mr. Jordash, you mentioned several names of people whom you come across in Eastern Slavonia. During this trial we have heard the names of two persons; I would like to check whether you're familiar with those names. Are you familiar with the names of Boro and Pujo? Do you know those names?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who they are.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Boro, his family name was Predragovic, and his first name is Borislav. And Momcilo Radovic is Pujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which service did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: They were members of the public security service. Momcilo Radovic belonged to the SUP of Novi Sad and Boro Predragovic was employed by the training centre in Sremska Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, my learned friend Mr. Jordash also asked you about training centres, and you mentioned training in Vukovar, in the Petrova Gora barracks. You said that the person in charge of that training was a soldier whose nickname was Kole. That's on pages 55 and 56. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. But his name was not Kostic, but Kovacevic. His nickname was Kole. He was an officer. He was a captain by rank. And he was a member of the Territorial Defence Staff. We were not the only ones who crossed over. There were also officers, and all the commanders of the TO were members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does the name Borislav Kostic ring a bell? Is that perhaps Kole?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Radoslav Kostic, Borislav Kostic. Radoslav Kostic was killed and the centre bore his name. What was the name? Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Borislav.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: It is possible that that was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That Kole whom you described as the person in charge of the training centre, did he sport a red beret?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: None of us wore red berets. And that includes him, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And now we will go back to the part of the examination-in-chief when Mr. Jordash asked you about Arkan's arrival at the crossing. If I understood you properly, the first time you told him to go back. And then on the following day he returned with a permission signed by Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic. Did he arrive in a vehicle, one or more? How many vehicles were there?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: He crossed over in jeeps of foreign make. You will see it in my statement there were three or four jeeps. Those were Pajero Jeeps, and he wore olive-drab American uniform or, rather, camouflage uniform. I don't know what to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Pajero Jeeps that he used, were those from civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You also mentioned, on page 49, lines 8, 9, and 10, that volunteers received salaries from their companies or institutions. Did I understand you properly? Did you say that those people who left Serbia and went to help people in these areas received monies from their companies or institutions?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes, they were paid regularly. They received salaries in the same way as if they worked for their companies. But they had to provide a certificate signed by Badza attesting to the fact that they were indeed deployed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was that done based on a regulation that prevailed in Serbia at the time regarding people who were volunteers and who were still to be paid from their companies?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I really don't know. I only know that they wanted us to provide the certificates. And as for any regulations, I'm not a man who follows regulations, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. What you don't know, you don't know, of course. Let's move on. And now let us look at Exhibit P1127. I am interested in the first paragraph. Let's wait for the document to be displayed. P1127, we have it now. Let us look at the first page and let us read the first paragraph. Tell me, please, whether you can see that this is a letter sent by the Vukovar SUP to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Knin. Please look at the first paragraph and tell me whether this reflects what you know about the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I cannot read. It's rather blurred. But judging by the date, I can say that at the time when this was issued, I wasn't there. I really don't know what I could say about the document because I was already in Becej and I proceeded with my regular tasks there. So I wasn't there on this particular date. As far as Arkan is concerned, I've already said several times that wherever he was, nobody could control him. He did whatever he deemed proper and correct. I can't read this. It's blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We heard you say that you can't say anything about this. It says here that on the 3rd of August, 1992, information was received about a special-purpose unit being established in Ermestinovo [phoen]. Its name would be Red Tigers. And it would be part of the 101st centre of the MUP of Serbian Krajina under the leadership of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I really can't comment. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to check whether you know anything about this. The second paragraph concerns a conflict between Kojic and Arkan. Since you mentioned that, I wanted to check whether you are aware of this conflict, but the period is not relevant -- irrelevant [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: As far as the conflict between Kojic and Arkan is concerned, that started on day one, from the moment when he crossed over with the permit. Ilija Kojic always expressed negative views of Arkan's deployment in Tenja and everywhere else. And those were not just Ilija's words. Those were the feelings of many other citizens who approached me with requests to send him back. But who was I to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two video-clips. I would like to finish my cross-examination with them. I am -- I believe that I could do that within the next ten minutes. We received those video-clips during our investigation or, rather, during the break from the person who made the video-clips available to us. We're still talking to that person, and with your permission we will like to propose the video-clip as an addition to our 65 ter list. These two video-clips are relative to the centre in Erdut. We wanted to show those two video-clips without any text in order to see whether the witness is in a position to provide any comments about those places. We don't have a transcript. But the text is not important. Mr. Farr wanted an explanation about the origin of the video-clips. With your permission, what we want to see is just the image. We would like to have them as 65 ter list exhibits at the moment. Later on, we can transcribe them and tender them in any other form. We are now in closed session. I can mention the name of the person who has provided the video-clips. He was a cameraman in the Serbian Volunteers Guard, in Arkan's unit. If this part of the trial is ever opened for public, I would kindly ask for this part to remain in closed session until the moment we see whether this person, the cameraman in question, requests protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. At this moment there's no need to decide on that. Mr. Farr, any further objections against showing the video without sound? And then if we only look at the pictures, I want the sound to be switched off so that the witness does not receive any information more than the Chamber and the non-B/C/S speaking persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The issue with respect to the video is simply that we haven't been able to see them yet. Ordinarily they would have been disclosed at the beginning of cross exam -- at the beginning of direct examination at the latest. But we're happy for them to be played. And then if we have an objection to admission, we can bring that up at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let the video be played. We've spent already -- you said there were two videos. If perhaps we start with the one. And perhaps we might need five more minutes tomorrow. But I would rather not add to my already bad reputation in going beyond time limits. The first video would be how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one, 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one. And could we ask the witness to take his earphones off so that there's no way that he would -- yes. Just look at your screen. And may the video be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you had not informed us that we would receive the full text at the bottom of the ... So do you read any English, Witness? Could you please put on your earphones again. Yes, can you read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now we are just in the opposite position, that now everyone has seen what has been said but that the witness apparently is unaware of it. Mr. Bakrac, put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the omission, Your Honours. I forgot to mention the titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise anybody in the clip?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: I didn't see a thing. I did not have the image on the screen at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's ... could it be replayed; and could -- it's only 40 seconds. But everyone is really trying to add to my bad reputation, I think. Could it be replayed. And could you take off your earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise the person with the bull horn?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you see people in uniforms with helmets whom he addresses?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you, based on this clip, recognise the formation that those individuals belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DST-074
utterances.text: These are military uniforms. JNA uniforms, to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I will show the next video-clip tomorrow morning. And all in all, I will need only ten minutes, and I will not have any more questions. I believe that I have done my utmost to improve your reputation, or repair it, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that, Mr. Bakrac. My reputation is saved by counsel. I highly appreciate that. We would like to see you back tomorrow, tomorrow morning, at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Meanwhile, you are instructed that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony or communicate in any other way, whether that is your testimony you have given today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow. Since we will adjourn in public session, I would like to invite you to follow the usher and leave the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 17th of August at 9.00 in the morning in this same Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of August, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
